limitations: Requires homogeneous isotropic propagation of light.
premises: Light propagation is isotropic and constant in all inertial frames.
arguments.question: When are two distant events simultaneous?

full.text: A ray of light emitted from A at time tA arrives at B at time tB and reflects back to A at time tA'.

margin.text: Einstein defines common time operationally through light transit.

overview.text: Clocks at A and B can be synchronized by sending light rays.

items: Emit light pulse from clock A at tA.
Reflect pulse at clock B at tB.
Receive return pulse at clock A at tA'.

arguments.recap: Simultaneity requires synchronized clocks linked by light signals.
arguments.title: Definition of Simultaneity

premises: Simultaneity is relative to the motion of the coordinate system.
arguments.question: Does length depend on the observer's motion?

full.text: The length of a moving rigid rod is contracted in the direction of motion.

margin.text: Contraction is kinematical rather than dynamical.

overview.text: A moving measuring rod has a contracted length in the stationary frame.

items: Measure rod in motion using synchronized clocks.

arguments.recap: Moving rods are measured to be shorter than stationary rods.
arguments.title: On the Relativity of Lengths and Times

premises: The laws of electrodynamics hold in all frames where mechanics holds.
arguments.question: How do electromagnetic fields transform between inertial frames?

full.text: The electromotive force on a charge in motion is the electric field in its rest frame.

margin.text: The asymmetry between magnet and conductor disappears.

overview.text: Electric and magnetic forces mix when changing frames.

items: Apply coordinate transformation to field derivatives.

arguments.recap: Maxwell equations retain their form under Lorentz transformation.
arguments.title: Transformation of Maxwell-Hertz Equations
